scripts.opening:opening:
[thoughtful] JAUNT: THE BRONZE AT EIGHTEENTH STREET. A Monday afternoon in November 1904, at the corner of Eighteenth Street and Prairie Avenue.

[short pause] Four stops round one street corner. There is a battlefield under the pavement, a bronze that tells a story about it, the house of the man who paid for the bronze, and the house that stared back at him. [short pause] [intrigued] Every stop is a question about what really happened, and who decided how it would be remembered.

[short pause] Start where the street starts: the ground where the battle was fought.
scripts.stop:ground: [solemnly] Prairie Avenue at Eighteenth Street. [short pause] Before the houses, this was sand hills by the lake. On 15 August 1812 the Battle of Fort Dearborn was fought across them, [softly] and the dead "lay in the sand, half buried where they were killed, until 1816". For a century a big cottonwood tree marked the spot. In 1900 a Tribune writer swore that the Pullman house in front of this corner "stands about where the massacre took place". [long pause] [lighter] Now look at the street in 1904: brick, granite, gas lamps, a schoolteacher bringing her class to see the sights. [short pause] The battle is ninety-two years gone, and it has become a lesson. [short pause] [pointedly] The question is who wrote the lesson. Walk east along Eighteenth Street to the bronze.
scripts.stop:bronze: [measured] The monument. George Pullman paid for it and set it up in 1893, near his own front door: Carl Rohl-Smith's bronze of the Potawatomi chief Black Partridge saving Margaret Helm, an officer's wife. [short pause] It is dramatic and noble, [pointedly] and it may never have happened. "Some historians regard the incident as the product of romantic imagination instead of eyewitness testimony", and they say "Mrs. Helm rode her horse to the shore of Lake Michigan where she found refuge." [short pause] The sculptor found his models at Fort Sheridan, among survivors of Wounded Knee, whom he called "Indians of the most untamed sort". [short pause] [wryly] One historian says the figures "may have owed more to Buffalo Bill Cody's Wild West Show than to actual research." [short pause] The teacher is reading the plaque aloud. Now look at the house the bronze stands guard over.
scripts.stop:strike: [measured] 1729 Prairie, the Pullman house. The man who paid for the bronze built sleeping cars, and a company town south of the city where his workers paid him rent. [short pause] In 1894 he cut their wages, but "he didn't reduce the rent in Pullman", [pointedly] and they struck. [short pause] [intrigued] And here is the twist the bronze cannot tell: "a year after the statue's dedication", the Seventh Cavalry, the regiment of Wounded Knee, "came to Chicago to quell the Pullman riots of 1894." [short pause] [darkly] The regiment came to Chicago to put down a strike against the man who had put a battle of 1812 at his door. [long pause] Pullman died in 1897. The house will be razed in 1922. Cross Prairie to the house that stared at his.
scripts.stop:grave: [wryly] The Glessner corner, diagonally across from Pullman. Pullman hated this house: [grumbling] "I do not know what I have ever done to have that thing staring me in the face every time I go out of my door". [short pause] He spent his last years between the bronze and the granite. [short pause] [softly] When he died, his family was afraid that his body would be dug up by robbers, or by men who had worked for him. They buried him in a "lead-lined mahogany coffin, which was then sealed inside a block of concrete", under steel rails "bolted together at right angles". [short pause] One historian is honest about the legends: "Whether it's true or not, we don't really know." [long pause] [thoughtful] That is the lesson of this corner. Bronze, granite and concrete, [softly] and under all of it... the sand.
scripts.ending:sand: [thoughtful] End of the walk. In 1904 the bronze still stands at Eighteenth Street, telling its story one way. [short pause] Some historians doubt the rescue it shows ever happened. Pullman lies at Graceland under his concrete, the strike he broke is in every history book, and the ground under this corner still holds the sand of 1812. [long pause] A monument tells you who paid for it. [short pause] [softly] The rest you have to dig for.
